summary.name: Observations on Observability
summary.one_liner: An essay by Colin Breck arguing that the software industry's use of "observability" (logging, tracing, metrics) misuses the control-theory term, and that operating software at scale will look more like process engineering using continuous telemetry.
use_cases: Understanding the critique of the term observability in software
Designing telemetry for streaming or message-based systems
Exploring control-theory approaches to operating software systems
Choosing metrics as continuous signals instead of per-request traces
Background reading for SRE and monitoring strategy
summary.what_it_does: The essay summarizes the current software observability narrative (instrumenting requests via logs, traces and metrics, with sampling and rich metadata) and contrasts it with the control-theory definition of observability, which relates to controllability. It argues that request-centric tracing is like pigging in pipelines and is limited for understanding complex systems in aggregate. It recommends recording fine-grained, low-cardinality counters (differentiated after the fact) as continuous signals. It proposes borrowing methods from process industries, such as PCA, statistical process control charts, MPC, PID-style control and design of experiments, for monitoring and controlling software systems.
notable: Argues that the term observability is misapplied from control theory and suggests alternatives such as visibility or discernibility
Uses oil pipeline pigging and refinery analogies to critique request-level tracing
Recommends recording counters and differentiating after the fact, citing Windows Performance Counters
Discusses PCA and statistical process control for multivariate monitoring
caveats: This is an opinion essay, not a tool; it describes no software product or implementation
The author admits the argument may seem pedantic and describes the proposed future as a prediction
